summary: Defines terminology and lists requirements for resolving the context of emergency calls placed over VoIP and Internet multimedia systems. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A list of what is needed so an emergency call over the internet can reach the right helpers.

questions: how are voip emergency calls routed
what is an emergency service urn
subtitle: What an Internet emergency call system must do to turn a caller's location into the right emergency answering point.

tldr.problem: Emergency calling built for the telephone network does not suit IP voice, text and video, where the access provider and the voice provider are often different parties.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines terminology and lists requirements for a mapping protocol that takes a caller's location and a service identifier and returns a PSAP URI, plus requirements for location, service identifiers and the overall architecture.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document, not a protocol. It mentions LoST as a proposed mapping protocol, and security threats are left to a separate document.

today: RFC 5012 is an Informational RFC from January 2008. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated; it lists requirements and does not define a protocol.

sections.title: Goals and Scope
sections.content:
Users of voice and non-voice services, including text for hearing-disabled users, expect to be able to ask for help in an emergency. The existing mechanisms from the circuit-switched telephone network (PSTN) do not suit IP-based voice, text and multimedia. The RFC lists the requirements IP end systems and network elements such as SIP proxies must meet to offer at least the same functions as the PSTN, while being more robust, cheaper to implement and multimedia-capable.

It covers only end-to-end IP calls, from an IP end system to an IP-capable public safety answering point (PSAP). The main output of the mapping protocol is a PSAP URI, such as a SIP or SIPS URI, based on location and a service identifier. Caller identification and the display of location to the PSAP are out of scope. The RFC 2119 words apply to the design of the mapping protocol, not to its implementation or use.
sections.plainLanguage: Calling for help should work for phone calls, texts and video over the internet, just like the old phone network, but better. The call must reach the right helpers for where you are.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
The RFC defines basic emergency service, where a caller reaches a PSAP serving the current location but the PSAP may not know where the caller is, and enhanced emergency service, where the call taker can determine the location. It separates provider roles: the Internet Access Provider (IAP) supplies layer 1 and 2 connectivity, the Internet Service Provider (ISP) supplies IP service, and the Application Service Provider (ASP) or Voice Service Provider (VSP) supplies call services.

Location can be civic (such as a street address) or geographic (coordinates, for example in the WGS-84 datum). Identifiers are kept distinct: the service number (such as 911 in the United States), the dial string (which may differ behind a PBX, for example 9911), the service identifier, and a service URN such as urn:service:sos. Mapping is resolving a location to one or more PSAP URIs, performed by a mapping client talking to a mapping server.
sections.plainLanguage: The note gives names to everyone involved: the caller, the company that brings the internet, the company that carries the call, and the helpers who answer.

sections.title: Actors and Call Routing
sections.content:
Figure 1 of the RFC shows the entities: the emergency caller, the Internet Access Provider, the Application/Voice Service Provider, a mapping service, an Emergency Service Routing Proxy (ESRP) and the PSAP. Since the IAP and the ASP/VSP are usually different entities, the ASP/VSP typically cannot learn the caller's physical location directly.

The location may come from the end host itself or from the IAP. The caller may consult the mapping service directly, or get help from an ESRP that calls the mapping service and then forwards the call to the PSAP. The caller may also interact with the PSAP directly after doing the mapping itself. Several roles may be collapsed into one entity, and end systems may act as their own ASP/VSP.
sections.plainLanguage: Many helpers pass the message along: the one who gives you internet, the one who carries your call, a map-reader, and the final dispatcher. Sometimes one helper does several jobs.

sections.title: High-Level and Location Requirements
sections.content:
Eight high-level requirements (Re1 to Re8) set the shape. Emergency calls SHOULD NOT assume a voice service provider exists, must work internationally, MUST NOT depend on a single central authority, and MUST support multiple media such as audio, video and text. The mapping protocol MUST return URIs usable in standard signaling, MUST work without enrollment in a mapping service, SHOULD use common location formats such as PIDF-LO, and MUST NOT require the caller's true identity.

Location can be UA-inserted, UA-referenced (a pointer to a location server) or proxy-inserted. Nine location requirements (Lo1 to Lo9) include support for the WGS-84 datum, by-value delivery of location, reporting the result of civic address validation, and support for 2D and 3D locations. Lo7 says successful validation MUST NOT be required to place an emergency call, so an unrecognized address must not cause a call to be dropped.
sections.plainLanguage: Rules say the system must work anywhere in the world, must not need one boss, and must let a call be text or video too. Even if the address looks odd, the call must still go through.

sections.title: Emergency Service Identifiers
sections.content:
Emergency service identifiers are protocol constants that let entities such as SIP proxies tell emergency calls from other calls and name the service wanted. Nine requirements (Id1 to Id9) cover them. The protocol MUST support different services such as fire, police and ambulance, MUST support an extensible list, and MUST be able to return the emergency number for a location.

User equipment MUST be able to translate a home emergency number into a service identifier, and signaling protocols MUST be able to mark a call as an emergency call. If a requested service is not recognized or not offered, the call MUST still be routed to a generic emergency service, and the mapping response MUST be able to report the substitute service. The protocol MUST also let a device learn visited emergency numbers when traveling.
sections.plainLanguage: A special label says this is an emergency, and what kind. If the exact helpers are not available, the call goes to a general emergency desk instead of getting lost.

sections.title: The Mapping Protocol
sections.content:
There are two ways to invoke mapping. In caller-based resolution the caller's user agent asks the mapping server, possibly well before the call. In mediated resolution a proxy or redirect server asks on its behalf. A proposed protocol, LoST, is mentioned. Seventeen requirements (Ma1 to Ma17) apply.

Key ones: a mandatory-to-implement baseline protocol, extensibility, incremental deployability (some misrouting is acceptable while databases are incomplete), mapping at any time and from anywhere, and routing to the PSAP responsible for the area. The protocol MUST support multiple PSAP URIs for the same area but SHOULD return only one primary URI per contact protocol, MAY return a less-preferred scheme such as a tel URI for non-IP PSAPs, and MUST support referral to a more qualified mapping server, split responsibility between servers, an error-reporting URL and failover to replica servers. It SHOULD allow tracing which servers answered, minimize call-setup delay with time-limited caching, and indicate freshness.

The RFC does not analyze security itself. It says threats and security requirements are discussed in a separate document, RFC 5069.
sections.plainLanguage: Either your phone looks up the right helpers on a map, or a helper in the middle does it for you. The map must keep working even if one map-keeper is down.

viz.caption: TWO WAYS TO INVOKE MAPPING (RFC 5012, SECTION 8)

left.title: Caller-based
left.desc: The caller's user agent asks for the PSAP, possibly well before the call.

right.title: Mediated
right.desc: A routing support entity such as a SIP proxy asks on the caller's behalf.
